id: ‘One morn I left him in his bed’

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

One morn I left him in his bed; A moment after some one said, ‘Your child is dying – he is dead.’ We made him ready for his rest, Flowers in his hair, and on his breast His little hands together prest. We sailed by night across the sea; So, floating from the world were we, Apart from sympathy, we Three. The wild sea moaned, the black clouds spread Moving shadows on its bed, But one of us lay midship dead. I saw his coffin sliding down The yellow sand in yonder town, Where I put on my sorrow’s crown. And we returned; in this drear place Never to see him face to face, I thrust aside the living race. Mothers, who mourn with me today, Oh, understand me, when I say, I cannot weep, I cannot pray; I gaze upon a hidden store, His books, his toys, the clothes he wore, And cry, ‘Once more, to me, once more!’ Then take, from me, this simple verse, That you may know what I rehearse— A grief – your and my Universe!

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your poem, preserving its structure, rhyme scheme, and all original content while refining the language for greater eloquence:

---

One morning I left him in his bed;
A moment after, someone said,
"Your child lies dying—he is dead."

We made him ready for his rest,
With flowers woven through his hair, and pressed
His small hands gently on his breast.

By night we sailed across the sea;
Thus, drifting from the world were we,
Beyond all sympathy, we Three.

The wild sea moaned, black clouds arrayed
Their shifting shadows o'er its bed,
Yet one among us, midship, lay dead.

I watched his coffin glide below,
Along the yellow sand's soft flow,
Where I first bore my crown of woe.

And so we returned; in this bleak place,
No more to see him face to face,
I turned aside from the living race.

Mothers who share my mourning today,
Oh, understand me when I say—
I cannot weep, I cannot pray;

I gaze upon his hidden store—
His books, his toys, the clothes he wore—
And cry, "Once more, oh, give me once more!"

Then take from me this simple verse,
That you may know what I rehearse—
A grief that is our shared Universe.

---

I preserved the original triplet rhyme scheme (aaa), the narrative sequence, and every detail (the flowers, the sea voyage, the coffin, the mother's anguish, and the closing address to fellow mourners), while refining word choices and phrasing for greater fluidity and emotional resonance.
outputs.L2:
One dawn I stepped from his bedside; Within moments, someone's voice replied, 'Your little one has passed, he died.' We dressed him for eternal peace, Blossoms woven through his hair, at least, His folded palms upon his breast released. Under darkness, we crossed the ocean's swell; Three souls drifting where no others dwell, Severed from all who might console us well. The restless waters cried, dark clouds hung low, Casting their shifting darkness to and fro, While one among us lay still, silent, so. I watched his casket lowered from above Into gold sand of that distant town's cove, Where I first wore the crown of loss and love. Homeward we came, to this bleak abode, Never again to walk life's shared road; I turned from living faces, bore my load alone.

Grieving mothers who share this same dark day, Hear what I confess, hear what I say— I cannot weep now, nor find words to pray; I stare instead at what remains concealed, His storybooks, his toys, the clothes he'd wield, And beg the emptiness: 'Return him, do not yield!'

Accept then this plain offering of mine, That you might recognize within each line— A sorrow vast as any universe, yours and mine entwined.
outputs.L3:
# The Morning He Was Taken

I left him sleeping in his bed that morning, his small chest rising and falling with the steady rhythm of a life that seemed as permanent as the sunrise. I kissed his brow, whispered words of ordinary tenderness—the kind we save unknowingly for the last time—and stepped away to face the day's demands. It could not have been more than an hour, perhaps less, before the word came to me like a blow from an unseen hand: my child was dead. The boy I had left alive, laughing perhaps, or murmuring in his sleep, had slipped away in that brief span between my leaving and my learning. There was no illness that had warned us, no lingering decline that might have prepared the heart for such a blow. He was simply, suddenly, gone.

## Preparing Him for the Earth

What followed passed in a haze of necessary motion, the body's instinct to *do* something when the mind cannot comprehend the why. We washed him gently, my wife and I, our hands trembling with a grief too large for words. We gathered flowers—white ones, I remember, though I could not tell you now what kind—and wove them around his small form, as if beauty might somehow soften what death had done. We folded his hands upon his chest, arranging them with a care that bordered on reverence, positioning his fingers as though he were merely at peaceful rest, as though prayer had simply overtaken him mid-breath. In that small, still face, we searched for some sign of the boy we knew, and in the arrangement of his body, we tried to grant him a dignity that our own hearts could not yet feel.

## The Crossing

Circumstance demanded that we travel, and so we set out to sea with our child's body carried between us like a secret too heavy for language. The night was wild with storm—waves crashing against the hull, wind screaming through the rigging—as if the very heavens grieved alongside us, or perhaps mocked our small human sorrow with their vast indifference. We stood apart from the other passengers, unable to speak of what we carried, unable to accept the ordinary kindness of strangers who did not know what lay wrapped below. We were islands unto ourselves in that heaving darkness, bound together by loss and separated from everyone else by a grief too private, too raw, to be shared with those who had not felt its weight.

## Burial in a Foreign Land

The ship brought us at last to a town whose name meant nothing to us, whose streets we walked as strangers even as we prepared to leave our son forever within its borders. There, in unfamiliar sand, we lowered the small coffin into ground that held no memory of him, no history that was ours. I stood at the edge of that grave and felt the full measure of what had been taken—not merely a child, but a future, a name that would carry forward, a small hand that would never again reach for mine. The foreignness of the place seemed to sharpen the sorrow, as if burying him among strangers made the loss more absolute, more final, than if we had laid him to rest among our own.

## The Long Silence After

When we returned home, I found I could not resume the shape of my former life. The company of the living felt unbearable—their small talk, their unbroken families, their ignorance of what true devastation felt like. I could not weep, though grief sat like a stone in my chest; I could not pray, though the words had once come easily to my lips. Instead, I turned to what remained: a small shoe, a worn toy, a scrap of cloth that still somehow carried his scent. These fragments became my only comfort, the only conversation I could bear to have with my sorrow.

And when other mothers came to me, broken as I was broken, seeking some words to hold against their own unbearable losses, I gave them this—these verses wrung from the depths of a grief that language could barely hold, offered not as healing, but as recognition. Perhaps in shared sorrow there is a kind of solace, though never a cure. Perhaps in knowing another has walked this same dark road, the weight becomes, if not lighter, then at least less lonely to bear.
outputs.L4:
# What the Sea Took

We put flowers in his hair
because we did not know
what else the living do
for those who leave so fast—
one morning breathing,
by noon, still.

The coffin was small.
Smaller than it should have been.
We watched it slide
down the sandy shore
the way children slide
in games we no longer play,
except this was no game,
and the shore did not laugh,
and the water did not clap.

The tide took him out
past where our eyes could follow,
past where our voices,
raw from calling his name
all night in the house,
could reach him now.

No one came.
Or perhaps they did,
and we did not see them,
wrapped as we were
in the small country of our grief,
a nation of two,
speaking a language
only losing a child
can teach you.

His mother said—
and I remember this exactly,
the way you remember
the worst thing ever spoken aloud—
she said: *I cannot cry.
I cannot pray.
The words for both
have left me,
the way he left,
without warning,
without permission.*

So she gathered instead
the small things he touched—
a shoe with no match,
a shirt still holding
the shape of his shoulders,
a toy worn smooth
by his particular hands—
and she held them
the way you hold
what refuses to be enough,
what will never be enough,
but is all
that remains to hold.

I tell you this
not because our sorrow
is different from yours,
not because the sea
took only our child,
but because it did not.
It has taken and will take
so many,
in so many houses,
in so many nights
where someone stands
holding a small shoe,
unable to cry,
unable to pray,
learning the same
terrible language
that every grieving mouth
eventually speaks—

the one where silence
is the only word
that means anything at all.
outputs.L5:
# One Garden, Your Story

There is something quietly powerful about the word *one*. One seed. One bloom. One moment of stillness in a hurried day. In a world that often measures worth by quantity—more tasks, more noise, more everything—the simplicity of one flower can feel like a small rebellion against the chaos.

Flowers have always carried meaning beyond their petals. They mark celebrations, soften grief, and speak when words fall short. But it's easy to overlook how much meaning a single flower can hold. A single rose says something different than a bouquet of a dozen. It says: *I thought of you specifically. Not the idea of flowers in general, but this one, chosen with care.*

This is where the personal comes in—**your** flowers, your garden, your relationship with growing things. Maybe it's a windowsill herb pot you've kept alive against all odds. Maybe it's a wildflower meadow you pass on your morning walk, the same patch you've watched change with the seasons for years. Whatever it is, it's yours. Not because you own the land or the bloom, but because you've given it attention, and attention is its own kind of belonging.

There's a lesson in tending to one flower at a time. Gardeners know that you can't rush a bloom. You can't will a bud open before it's ready. This patience, this respect for the plant's own rhythm, is a kind of quiet wisdom that spills over into how we might approach the rest of our lives. One step. One breath. One flower, fully seen, rather than a hundred glanced over.

So perhaps the invitation is this: find your one flower. Not the grandest, not the rarest, but the one that means something to you. Let it be a small anchor—a reminder that meaning doesn't require abundance, only presence. Your flower doesn't need to impress anyone. It simply needs to be seen, cared for, and allowed to bloom in its own time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style elegy in triplet stanzas (aabccb rhyme) about a mother mourning the death of her young child during a sea voyage.
counterfactuals.output:
# A Requiem for the Deep

The ship rocked soft upon the deep,
Where restless waves their vigil keep,
And moonlight paved a silver way—
Beneath the sail a mother pressed
Her infant to her weary breast,
And prayed the dark would gently stay.

But fever walked with quiet tread,
And touched the small and drowsy head,
Where once had danced a merry glow—
The little limbs, so warm before,
Grew still and chill upon the floor
Of that dark cabin, rocking slow.

No physic's art, no mother's prayer,
Could stay the hand of dark despair;
He came as calm as fall of night,
And laid his touch upon the brow,
And closed the eyes that dimmed by now,
And quenched at once their living light.

They wrapped him in a sailor's shroud,
No bell was rung, no mourner's crowd,
Only the wind to breathe a prayer;
They bore him to the vessel's side,
Where deep and dark the waters bide,
And gave him to the ocean's care.

The mother stood with hollow eyes,
And watched beneath the empty skies
The water close above his head—
No little cross, no mound of earth,
To mark the place that knew his birth
Unto a life so quickly fled.

Now every wave that rocks the ship
Seems but the cradle's gentle dip,
And every wind a lullaby;
She hears his laughter in the foam,
She seeks him still in every home
Of cloud that wanders down the sky.

Sleep, little one, beneath the wave,
Thy cradle now shall be thy grave,
Till trumpets wake the sea and shore;
Then shall the deep give up her dead,
And every tear be comforted,
And love shall hold thee evermore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a mournful poem, using rhyming triplets, from the perspective of a grieving parent describing burying their child at sea and returning home to a "drear place."
counterfactuals.output:
**The Sea Took What I Loved**

We carried you where grey waves roll and heave,
No churchyard earth to dig, no soil to grieve,
Only salt water there to receive.

The sailors bowed their heads and spoke no word,
The only sound the wind and crying bird,
And in my chest, a silence no one heard.

I watched you slip beneath the foam and swell,
No stone to mark, no name for me to tell,
Just water closing like a tolling bell.

The captain said a prayer, brief and plain,
The ship sailed on through sun and salted rain,
While something in me broke and stayed in pain.

We turned the bow toward home, though home was gone,
For what is home when one dear soul has flown,
And I must walk these empty halls alone?

I climbed the steps I climbed a hundred times,
Recalling all your laughter, all your rhymes,
Now silent as the tolling funeral chimes.

Your room stands still, your small shoes by the door,
I cannot bear to see them anymore,
Yet cannot make myself to shut that door.

The hearth is cold, the kettle does not sing,
The house forgets the joy that you would bring,
And I forget the reason for anything.

I set your place at table out of pain,
Then weep to see it empty once again,
A private ritual of shattered brain.

The clock ticks on as if the world's the same,
As if my world has not gone up in flame,
As if I still recall my own name.

They tell me time will dull this wretched ache,
That I will learn to breathe, to eat, to wake,
But every dawn's a wound that will not break.

I keep your picture near the windowsill,
And watch the harbor where the fishing boats spill,
Wondering if the sea remembers still.

Does the water cradle you at night?
Do the currents hold you soft and tight?
Does something living keep you warm and bright?

I do not know, I only know this grief,
This drear house, this ash without relief,
This endless winter with no autumn leaf.

The sea has you, and I have but this shore,
This empty house, this silence, and this door
That opens now to nothing, evermore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a sad, old-fashioned poem about losing a child, incorporating imagery of a coffin, a sea voyage, and a mother's inability to weep or pray afterward?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Voyage Home

The carpenter came at break of dawn,
His hammer soft, his face drawn long,
To build a box so small and white—
No child should sail on such a night.

They laid thee down in linen fair,
With rosebuds twined amongst thy hair,
And closed the lid upon thy face,
That once did fill this empty place.

We bore thee to the harbor's edge,
Where grey gulls cried along the ledge,
And placed thee on the outbound ship
That carries souls past sorrow's lip.

The sails went up like folded hands,
The vessel left these weeping lands,
And I stood rooted to the shore
Long after I could see no more.

They tell me I should kneel and pray,
That God attends the words we say,
But heaven seems a distant door
I cannot find, nor reach, nor implore.

They tell me tears would ease this weight,
Would soften grief, would help me wait—
But something in me turned to stone
The moment that they called me "own"

Referring to the past, not thee,
As if thou wert a memory
Already, though the ship's still bound
For shores where lost things may be found.

I do not weep. I cannot pray.
I only watch the water's spray
And wonder if, upon that tide,
Thou knowest that thy mother died

A little, when they shut that lid—
Not screaming, as the grief-struck did,
But quiet, like a candle's end,
No prayer to speak, no tear to spend.

The ship has long gone past the bend.
I stand here still. I cannot mend.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poignant, archaic-language poem in three-line rhyming stanzas that captures a parent's grief after their child dies suddenly and is buried during a voyage across the ocean.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Lament for a Child Lost at Sea**

We sailed upon the salt grey deep,
My babe was nestled soft in sleep,
And o'er us watched the stars did keep.

The wind did sing a gentle song,
The waves did bear the ship along,
And naught did seem to us go wrong.

But ere the third day's light had come,
A fever seized my little one,
And all the joy of life was done.

His cheeks that once did bloom so red
Grew pale as linen on the bed,
And ere the dawn, my child was dead.

O captain, stay thy vessel's course,
For grief hath weight, and grief hath force,
And I would weep till I grow hoarse.

They wrapped him in a canvas shroud,
No bell did toll, no mourner's crowd,
Only the wind that moaned aloud.

A prayer was said, so brief, so plain,
Then given he unto the main,
And ne'er was I made whole again.

The water closed without a sound,
No stone to mark, no hallowed ground,
Only the deep, so vast, unbound.

I stood upon the creaking deck
And watched the wave, a fading speck,
Bear off my heart, my life, my wreck.

Now every swell that meets the bow
Doth seem to murmur of him now,
And press fresh sorrow on my brow.

I search the foam for some small sign,
Some token still to call him mine,
But find no comfort in the brine.

We reached at last the far-off shore,
Yet empty were these arms I bore,
For he sleeps where the deep does roar.

O sea, thou keeper of my son,
Guard well the soul thy waves have won,
Till Judgment's trumpet call be done.

And when at last my days shall cease,
And I am granted my release,
God grant I find my babe in peace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem addressed to other grieving mothers, expressing shared sorrow over a child's death, ending with an offering of "this simple verse" as a token of universal grief.
counterfactuals.output:
# To Sisters in Sorrow

You who have felt the weight I carry now,
The empty room, the silence where a voice
Once filled the air with laughter—you will know
This grief that leaves no room for other choice.

We did not choose this sisterhood of pain,
Were never asked if we could bear the cost.
Yet here we stand, bound by a common chain,
Each mourning what the world has coldly lost.

I see you in the store, in aisles bright,
Reach for a toy before the memory stings.
I see you wake at 3 a.m. each night,
Listening for sounds no longer there to bring.

Do you, too, keep a small shoe by the door?
Do you, too, speak to photographs on walls?
Do you, too, wonder what they had in store—
The years unlived, the unheard, growing calls?

There is no measure deep enough to hold
The weight of what we've lost, what we still love.
No timeline promises the ache turns cold,
No greater plan we're meant to be thinking of.

But in this valley, we are not alone—
Though miles and names and circumstance divide,
Each mother knows this sorrow as her own,
Each carries what no words can say inside.

So take my hand across the distance wide,
Let grief connect what language cannot reach.
I cannot heal the wound that lives inside,
But I can offer what my heart would teach:

That love does not expire with the breath,
That children live in every act we do,
That even shadowed by the weight of death,
We mother still—in memory, we're true.

For every mother here who's lost a child,
Who knows this darkness no one else can see,
I offer up these words, however mild—
This simple verse, as gift, from me to thee.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
